en: The Sūtra on the Definitive Meaning of the Dharma-Vehicle, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Mingyin Miaoshan Pujie,
Jin Zongchi, and others, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove Monastery, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Gambhīravīra, who possessed a beautiful and melodious voice and was skilled in inquiring about the essential points of the Dharma—excellent in its beginning, middle, and end—which benefits both oneself and others. Being able to cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya) in a pure and perfect manner, he paid homage with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the definitive meaning of the Dharma-vehicle taught by the Tathāgata in the past at the Deer Park— what is the nature of this matter?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain it clearly and reveal it to sentient beings, so that all may awaken to and enter into it!
The World-Honored One praised him, saying: "Excellent, bhikṣu!
That you should thus inquire after such profound essentials of the Dharma brings the most supreme benefit, inconceivable in its measure. You should listen attentively and reflect upon it well!"
I shall now analyze and explain this for you.
At that time, when I preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, its meaning was inexhaustible. That is to say:

the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*), the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), the four noble truths, the twenty-two faculties (*dvāviṃśati-indriya*), the five samādhis, the four dhyāna heavens, the four formless attainments (*catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ*), the four samādhis, the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*), the five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*), the five powers (*pañca balāni*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta bodhyaṅgāni*), the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), the sixteen mental applications, the four fruits of the śrāvaka, the ten powers of a Tathāgata (*daśa tathāgatabalāni*), the four fearlessnesses (*catvāri vaiśāradyāni*), the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*), the eighteen unique qualities (*aṣṭādaśāveṇikabuddhadharmāḥ*), the thirty-two marks of a great man (*dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇāni*), and the eighty minor marks (*aśītyanuvyañjanāni*).
The Buddha said:
“Monks! As explained above, this is called the definitive meaning of the Dharma-vehicle.”
The bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what are the five aggregates?”
The Blessed One replied:
"They are the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness, bhikṣu."
"These are called the five aggregates.
"What are the five aggregates of clinging?
The Buddha said:

"They are the aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregate of clinging to feeling, the aggregate of clinging to perception, the aggregate of clinging to formations, and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness. Monks,
these are called the five aggregates of clinging."
“What are the twelve bases? The Buddha said:
“That is to say, the eye is the internal base, and visible forms are the external base;”
The ear is an internal sense base, and sound is an external sense base;
the nose is an internal sense base, and odor is an external sense base;
the tongue is an internal sense base, and taste is an external sense base.
The body is an internal sense base and tangibles are an external sense base;
the mind is an internal sense base and mental phenomena are an external sense base. Monks!
"These are called the twelve bases (āyatana).
What are the eighteen elements (dhātu)?
The Buddha said:
That is to say: the eye-element, the form-element, and the eye-consciousness-element;
the ear-element, the sound-element, and the ear-consciousness-element;
the nose-element, the odor-element, and the nose-consciousness-element;
The tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element;
the body element, the tangible object element, and the body-consciousness element;
the mind element, the mental object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
“Monks! These are called the eighteen elements (dhātus).
“What are the twelve factors of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda)?”
The Buddha said:
"That which is called 'ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness';"
Consciousness conditions name-and-form;
name-and-form conditions the six sense bases;
the six sense bases condition contact.
Contact conditions feeling;
feeling conditions craving;
craving conditions clinging.
With grasping as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises;
with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair arise.
With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease;
with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases;
with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases.
With the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease;
with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases;
with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases.
With the cessation of feeling, craving ceases;
with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases;
with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases.
With the cessation of existence, birth ceases;
with the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair cease. Monks!
"These are called the twelve links of dependent origination.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is meant by 'ignorance' (avidyā)?
The World-Honored One replied,
"It refers to delusion and confusion that obscure and veil one's vision, because there is no other clear wisdom."
Lack of knowledge regarding the past; lack of knowledge regarding the future; lack of knowledge regarding the present; lack of knowledge regarding the internal;
lack of knowledge regarding the external; lack of knowledge regarding both the internal and the external;
lack of knowledge regarding karma; lack of knowledge regarding its fruit; and lack of knowledge regarding both karma and its fruit.
Lack of wisdom regarding wholesome actions; lack of wisdom regarding unwholesome actions;
lack of wisdom regarding the cause, lack of wisdom regarding the fruit, and lack of wisdom regarding the dharma of cause and fruit;
lack of wisdom regarding conditions, lack of wisdom regarding dependent origination, and lack of wisdom regarding the dharma of dependent origination.
There is no wisdom regarding the Buddha, no wisdom regarding the Dharma, and no wisdom regarding the Saṅgha;
there is no wisdom regarding suffering, no wisdom regarding its origin, no wisdom regarding its cessation, and no wisdom regarding the path;

there is no wisdom regarding shame, no wisdom regarding lack of shame, no wisdom regarding both shame and lack of shame, and no wisdom regarding the phenomena of shame and lack of shame, up to and including no wisdom regarding the phenomena of shame and lack of shame within the factors of craving.
Lack of wisdom regarding the mundane, lack of wisdom regarding the supramundane, and lack of wisdom regarding both mundane and supramundane phenomena;

lack of wisdom regarding that which is based on [clinging], lack of wisdom regarding that which is not based on [clinging], and lack of wisdom regarding phenomena that are both based on and not based on [clinging];
lack of wisdom regarding the conditioned, lack of wisdom regarding the unconditioned, and lack of wisdom regarding both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.
Ignorance regarding the past, ignorance regarding the present, ignorance regarding the future, and ignorance regarding the phenomena of the past, present, and future— monks,
this is called ignorance (avidyā).
“What is ‘with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise’?
The Buddha said:
“They are what are called bodily formations, verbal formations, and mental formations.”
"This is called 'conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise. What are bodily formations?
They are the movements and activities performed; the body serves as the means for crossing over, it sustains all phenomena, and it acts as the locus of reliance."
"This is called bodily activity. What is verbal activity?
It is that which can express and reveal the true nature of all phenomena through differentiation and analysis."
"This is called verbal activity.
"What is mental activity? "That which the mind delights in, that which the mind contemplates, that which the mind grasps, and that upon which the mind relies."
"This is called mental activity.
[The Venerable Ānanda asked: "How is it that volitional formations condition consciousness? The Buddha said:
"Namely, eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
Monks! This is called 'conditioned by formations is consciousness.'"
“What is the conditionality of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) by way of consciousness?
The Buddha said:
“Name refers to the four aggregates that are non-material (arūpin):”
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"Form" refers to physical substance; its essence consists of the four great elements.
This is called "consciousness conditions name-and-form."
“What are the four great elements?
The Buddha said:
“They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.”
“What are the distinctions between the essential characteristics of the four great elements?
They are as follows: earth has solidity as its nature; water has moisture as its nature; fire has heat as its nature; and wind has lightness and motion as its nature.”
“Monks! This is called the differentiation of the essential characteristics of the four great elements.
What is meant by ‘with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise’?”
The Buddha said:
"They are the sense-base of the eye, the sense-base of the ear, the sense-base of the nose, the sense-base of the tongue, the sense-base of the body, and the sense-base of the mind."
“Monks! This is called ‘with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases.
How is it that ‘with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises’?”
The Buddha said:
“They are what are called eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact, bhikṣu.”
"This is called 'the six sense bases as condition for contact.
What is 'contact as condition for feeling'?
The Buddha said:
"What is called 'feeling born of eye-contact' refers to the arising of painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
It is the same for feelings born of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact."
“Monks! This is called ‘feeling conditioned by contact.
The monks again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that feeling conditions craving?
The Buddha said:
"They are attachment to forms, attachment to sounds, attachment to odors, attachment to tastes, attachment to tangibles, and attachment to mental phenomena. "What is attachment to forms?
"It refers to all that possesses form which is lovely and delightful, to which one is deeply attached in the heart and from which there is no weariness or detachment."
This is called craving for form.
Craving for sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena is likewise. Monks!
"This is called 'feeling as condition for craving.
What is 'craving as condition for clinging'?
The Buddha said:
"Namely, the grasping for sensual pleasures, the grasping for views, the grasping for precepts and observances, and the grasping for the doctrine of self.
Monks! This is called 'clinging conditioned by craving'."
“What is existence conditioned by grasping?
The Buddha said,
“It refers to existence in the realm of desire, existence in the realm of form, and existence in the formless realm.”
“What is sensual existence?

It refers to the five destinies of the desire realm, as well as the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.”
"This is called the existence of desire (*kāmadhātu-bhava*).
What is the existence of form (*rūpadhātu-bhava*)?
The Buddha said:

That is to say: the Brahmakāyika devas, the Brahmapurohita devas, the Mahābrahmā devas, the Parīttābha devas, the Apramāṇābha devas, the Ābhāsvara devas, the Parīttaśubha devas, the Apramāṇaśubha devas, the Śubhakṛtsna devas, the Anabhraka devas, the Puṇyaprasava devas, the Bṛhatphala devas, the Avṛha devas, the Atapa devas, the Sudṛśa devas, the Sudarśana devas, and the Akaniṣṭha devas.
"Monks! This is called existence with form.
What is existence without form?"
The Buddha said:
"They are the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
These are called the formless existence."
“Monks! These three kinds are called ‘existence conditioned by clinging.
“What is ‘birth conditioned by existence’?”
The Buddha said:

"What are called 'all sentient beings' arise through craving and grasping as conditions; they moisten the five aggregates for rebirth, abide in worldly activity, and follow along in the cycle of transmigration with various distinctions. Both what is given and what is taken all arise from the aggregates; they are produced by the body, having life as their root."
"Monks! This is called 'birth conditioned by existence.
"What is 'aging and death conditioned by birth'?"
The Buddha said:

"What is called the transformation of the four great elements, the decay of the sense faculties, the physical weakness of the body, becoming exhausted at the slightest movement, and the dulling of even vast learning and extensive knowledge."

For all sentient beings, when the body and consciousness are about to depart, the sense faculties are about to cease, and the nature of the objective realm becomes obscure and dark, such that there is nothing to be perceived or known.
Bhikṣu! This is called "old age and exhaustion conditioned by birth."
The bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the dharmas of the Four Noble Truths?”
The Buddha said:

"They are the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
"What is the noble truth of suffering?"

They are: the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of decay, the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.
"Monks! This is called the noble truth of suffering.
"What is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?"
The Buddha said:
“It is because sentient beings are attached to all that exists in the world and the requisites for existence, following after craving.
Bhikṣus!...”
"This is called the Dharma of the Truth of the Origin of Suffering.
[The interlocutor asked: "What is the Dharma of the Truth of Suffering itself? The Buddha said:

That is to say, by means of the sword of wisdom, one severs all attachment to the world, including both existence (*bhava*) and the instruments of existence (*bhavopakaraṇa*); following the exhaustion of craving without remainder, one enters the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) and realizes the principle of cessation (*nirvāṇa*).
"This is called the Dharma of the Noble Truth of Suffering.
[The Venerable Ānanda asked: "What is the Dharma of the Noble Truth of the Path leading to the Cessation of Suffering? The Buddha said:
"The so-called eight factors of the noble path:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right mindfulness, right concentration, and right effort."
"This is called the Dharma of the Truth of the Path Leading to Suffering.
[The Venerable Ānanda asked: "What are the twenty-two faculties?
The Buddha said:
"The so-called five faculties beginning with the eye are: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body;
the five faculties beginning with faith are: faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom;
the five feeling faculties are: suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity."

The three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya)— namely, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñātavya-ājñendriya), the faculty of "one who has known" (ājñendriya), and the faculty of "one who has fully known" (ājñātāvīndriya)—
as well as the mental faculty (manas), the life faculty (jīvita), the male faculty (puruṣa), and the female faculty (strī). O Bhikṣu!
"These are called the twenty-two faculties.
"What are the five samādhis? The Buddha said:
"Regarding the limbs and five parts of the body, which are lovely and delightful, unmarred and uninjured, one develops deep attachment and feels love and joy toward the entire body."
Due to such a mind, one follows along with defiled desires and various attachments; failing to understand that things are illusory, one falsely clings to them as real.

Therefore, one should observe them according to reality: these five aggregates all arise from the conjunction of the four great elements. Contemplating this with a single mind, one dwells securely in the realization of the sublime samādhi known as the "wisdom of the concentration on the body."
It is like water scattered from atop a mountain that flows downward and spreads in the four directions; once it has spread thus, the water is no longer seen, and the ground becomes parched again.
At that time, a celestial being announces from mid-air:
"If you require water, I have a great celestial spring; it wells up spontaneously, pure, cool, and most delightful. It provides relief and nourishment, never exhausting."
“The arising of certain knowledge regarding the body brings infinite benefit; it is just like this!
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should reflect with careful discernment, observe, and deliberate upon this body as being unreal; you must not harbor attachment to it.”

For example, it is like the udumbara flower, the padma flower, the kumuda flower, and the puṇḍarīka flower—these four kinds of lotuses, blue, yellow, red, and white, which are of exquisite colors and exceedingly lovely; all are born from water and perish in water.
This body, subject to transformation, illusory and unreal, is likewise so!
Again, he addressed the bhikṣus:

“With the actions of body, speech, and mind fully purified, having attained resolute conviction, one dwells as they truly are in the gateways of samādhi; with a pure mind, one contemplates that all bodies are entirely without solidity.”
For example, suppose an elder or an elder’s son adorns his body with various rare jewels and new, clean, exquisite garments; although his appearance may be beautiful, his physical form is not solid.
However, if one can adorn oneself with pure actions of body, speech, and mind, this is called being solid.
Again, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“Observe in this manner and contemplate it well!

This body, with its five limbs, is conditioned and impermanent; within the four modes of deportment—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—one should maintain mindfulness and reflection, and firmly embrace pure concentration and wisdom.”
“Monks! These are called the five samādhis.
The monks again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the stages of the four dhyāna concentrations?
The Buddha said:
That which is called the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion is so called because it is free from all defilements of sensual desire and all afflictions;
the stage of joy and bliss born of concentration is so called because, having already abandoned applied and sustained thought, it has subdued obstructive defilements;
and the stage of sublime bliss free from joy is so called because one dwells securely in skillful means, performing deeds that bring benefit and happiness.

In the stage of purity of equanimity and mindfulness, having already transcended pleasure and pain, with wholesome and unwholesome states of mind subdued, one experiences neither suffering nor pleasure; because mindfulness is free from attachment, through skillful cultivation, it becomes perfectly pure.
“Monks! These are called the four stages of dhyāna-concentration.
“What are the four formless concentrations?”
The Buddha said:

"That which is called the concentration of the sphere of infinite space is so named because all perceptions of form have been completely transcended, and the mind is maintained in equanimity, dwelling in accordance with reality;
the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness is so named because one dwells in accordance with reality within the boundlessness of internal consciousness."
The concentration of the sphere of nothingness is so called because all phenomena are entirely non-existent;
the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is so called because coarse perception does not exist, yet subtle perception is not non-existent.
“Monks! These are called the four formless attainments.
At that time, the monks again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are called the four immeasurable minds?
The Buddha said:

"They are the immeasurable mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), the immeasurable mind of compassion (*karuṇā*), the immeasurable mind of sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and the immeasurable mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
What is called the immeasurable mind of loving-kindness?"

"It means that at all times and in all places, one follows with a mind of loving-kindness, benefiting sentient beings, not harming others, and being free from all enmity and resentment. With a vast and impartial mind, one treats all beings equally, cherishing and protecting them as if they were one's own infant. Without making distinctions between enemies and kin, one causes them to sever their fetters and hindrances, so that all may attain liberation."
This is called the immeasurable mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
It is the same for the minds of compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), O bhikṣus!
These are called the four immeasurable minds.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of suffering and happiness that should all be thoroughly understood:
namely, understanding manifold suffering, understanding the existence of suffering, understanding manifold happiness, and understanding the existence of happiness.
“What is meant by ‘thoroughly understanding all suffering’?

It refers to observing a certain type of person—one who is attached through greed, attached through hatred, and attached through delusion—who does not fear greed, and consequently gives rise to suffering, grief, and lamentation in accordance with that greed; who does not fear hatred, and consequently gives rise to suffering, grief, and lamentation in accordance with that hatred;
[and who does not fear delusion, and consequently gives rise to suffering, grief, and lamentation in accordance with that delusion].”
He is not afraid of delusion; he fully understands that because of delusion, suffering, grief, and lamentation arise in succession.

He diligently cultivates the five mundane roots of goodness—namely, the root of faith, the root of energy, the root of mindfulness, the root of concentration, and the root of wisdom—and successively attains the gateways of samādhi; such a person is called a bhikṣu who has exhausted the outflows.
This is called "knowing suffering. What is meant by "knowing the existence of suffering"?

It refers to observing a certain type of person who has little greed, little hatred, and little delusion; yet, because they do not fear the faults of even slight greed, they give rise to suffering, grief, and sorrow in accordance with it.
Although they possess only a slight degree of anger, they do not fear the faults of anger, and thus give rise to suffering, grief, and lamentation in accordance with it;

although they possess only a slight degree of delusion, they do not fear the faults of delusion, and thus give rise to suffering, grief, and lamentation in accordance with it—all of which they fully understand.
By diligently cultivating the five kinds of supramundane roots of goodness, one sequentially attains the gateways of samādhi and is called a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted.
This is what is called "knowing that there is suffering.
What is meant by "knowing all forms of happiness"?

It refers to a certain individual who thoroughly understands that these three unwholesome roots—greed, hatred, and delusion—are the fundamental causes for the arising of suffering, and who is able to eradicate them forever. Diligently cultivating the five kinds of untainted wholesome roots, such as faith and so forth, pertaining to the supramundane, they successively attain the gateways of samādhi; such a person is called a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted.
This is called the thorough knowledge of all forms of happiness.
Having thoroughly known the existence of happiness, one practices with diligent effort and successively attains the gateways of samādhi, as described above.
“Monks! These four kinds of suffering and pleasure should all be thoroughly understood.
The monks again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the names of the four samādhis?
The Buddha said:
That is to say: by means of faith, understanding, and upholding, practicing in accordance with the Dharma, one is able to sever craving;
by means of faith, understanding, and upholding, practicing in accordance with the Dharma, one penetrates all sublime gateways of the Dharma;
by means of faith, understanding, and upholding, practicing in accordance with the Dharma, one attains all profound wisdom and vision.
"Because by having faith, understanding, and upholding [the teaching], and practicing according to the Dharma, one attains all pure and wondrous wisdom.
"How can one sever craving? The Buddha said:
“Monks! You should, in an open space, or among the woods, or at the foot of a tree, or in a secluded place, remain constantly seated and not lying down, abiding in meditative concentration;

you should contemplate this body as being composed of a combination of thirty-six elements, its substance being impure, illusory, and unreal. You should not give rise to false thoughts of affection or attachment; contemplating in this way, you should develop a profound sense of weary detachment.”
“Monks! This is called being able to sever craving.
What are the thirty-six things?”
The Buddha said:
"What are called the twelve external characteristics?
They are: hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, eye discharge, tears, earwax, nasal mucus, saliva, filth and sweat, and the excrement, urine, and feces."
The twelve intermediate characteristics are:
skin, flesh, blood, muscle, sinew, veins, bone, marrow, fat, grease, brain, and membranes.
The twelve internal characteristics are:
The spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, liver, gallbladder, viscera, stomach, the two types of phlegm—red and white—and the two types of receptacles—raw and cooked.
Bhikṣus! These are called the thirty-six items.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
"Moreover, among all things produced from the earth in the world, such as the various grains and crops, they must depend upon plowing and sowing; they do not arise naturally and purely."
Therefore, you should dwell with a single-minded focus in an open space or beneath a forest tree, observing this body as it truly is: impure, false, and fragile;
its faculties, such as the eyes and ears, are constantly defiled, lacking solidity, and utterly loathsome. Thus, you should cultivate a sense of weary detachment.
"Abiding thus in the gateways of samādhi, one should have faith-understanding and uphold them, practicing according to the Dharma to forever sever craving.
How does one penetrate all the sublime gateways of the Dharma?"
The Buddha said, “Bhikṣus! You should, in open spaces,

beneath forest trees, or in secluded places, constantly sit without reclining, practice meditative concentration, and with mindfulness and compassion for all sentient beings, act as their guides so that they may all attain realization.”
All conditioned phenomena are illusory and unreal; they are like the udumbara flower, which, though its color is exquisite, cannot remain firm once it has blossomed.
This body is likewise not solid.

Therefore, you should dwell in meditative concentration in open spaces, beneath forest trees, or in secluded places, contemplating that the entire body is conditioned and unreal, like a dream or an illusion; through skillful means, you should instruct and guide sentient beings so that they all come to believe and accept it, and take delight in meditative concentration.
“Monks! This is called having faith-understanding and upholding samādhi, practicing in accordance with the Dharma, and penetrating all sublime dharma-gates.
“How does one obtain all profound wisdom and vision?”
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

“Abiding securely in meditative concentration, having awakened to this profound and subtle Dharma, they cherish it with deep resolve, remaining firm and resolute. Day and night they maintain focused mindfulness, practicing with diligence and without slackening; the light of their wisdom shines everywhere, so that the darkness of ignorance is forever extinguished without remainder.”
For example, when the sky is shrouded by dense clouds, if at midday those clouds suddenly disperse, the sunlight can be seen shining everywhere upon all things without obstruction;
likewise, the light of omniscience from the gateways of samādhi removes the obscurations of afflictions and ignorance in the same way.
Therefore, you should reflect upon this well, abide in accordance with reality, and without slackening day or night, firmly embrace all-knowledge. Monks!
"This is called having faith, understanding, and upholding the gateways of samādhi, practicing according to the Dharma, and thereby attaining all profound wisdom and vision.
"How does one attain all pure, wondrous wisdom?"
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"You should, in an open space, or beneath a forest tree, or in a secluded and quiet place, always sit without reclining. Abiding in right mindfulness within the gate of samādhi, because you have already become detached from painful feelings, pleasant feelings, sorrowful feelings, joyful feelings, and equanimous feelings, you shall cultivate supreme concentration until it is perfected and pure. Thus, you will dwell securely in the four samādhis, fully comprehend the four kinds of resolute understandings, embrace and penetrate them, and become great guides."

Whether one is a recipient or one who has attained realization, they abide in the stage of excellent equanimity, observing and evaluating the knowledge of all modes of being (*sarvajñajñāna*) in this very way, and in this very way!
Again, he addressed the bhikṣus:

“You should, in an open space, or at the foot of a forest tree, or in a secluded and quiet place, because you have already left behind suffering, left behind pleasure, left behind sorrow, left behind joy, and left behind equanimity, dwell as they truly are in the four samādhis—liberation through superior concentration, perfect and pure.”
“Monks! This is called having faith, understanding, and upholding the gateways of samādhi, practicing according to the Dharma, and thereby attaining all pure and wondrous wisdom. Monks!”
"These are called the four samādhis.
Thus ends the first fascicle of the *Buddhabhāṣita-dharmayāna-artha-viniścaya-sūtra*.
[The second fascicle of the *Buddhabhāṣita-dharmayāna-artha-viniścaya-sūtra* begins.]
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Mingyin Miaoshan Pujie Dharma Master,
Jin Zongchi, and others, by Imperial Decree. At that time,
the Bhikṣu Extremely Profound Courage again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘dwelling in the four foundations of mindfulness’?
The Buddha said:

“Monks! One should dwell contemplating the body internally, the body externally, and the body both internally and externally; being aware with right mindfulness of the impurity of form and the sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction of the entire world.

One should dwell contemplating feelings internally, feelings externally, and feelings both internally and externally; being aware with right mindfulness of the various sufferings and the sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction experienced by the entire world.”

One dwells observing the internal mind, the external mind, and both the internal and external mind as illusory and impermanent; one understands with right mindfulness all the world’s sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction.

One dwells observing internal phenomena, external phenomena, and both internal and external phenomena, awakening to the principle of non-self; one understands with right mindfulness all the world’s sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction.
“Monks! This is called abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness.
The monks again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the four right efforts?
The Buddha said:
That is to say: regarding unwholesome states that have not yet arisen, one uses the power of diligence to subdue and eliminate them, so that they never arise again;
regarding unwholesome states that have already arisen, one uses the power of diligence to subdue and eliminate them, so that they are forever extinguished;
and regarding wholesome states that have not yet arisen, one uses the power of diligence and right mindfulness to embrace them, so that they are brought into being.
Because one causes wholesome states that have already arisen to remain firm and stable through the power of diligence, to be sustained by right mindfulness, and to increase—
these are called the four right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇa*).
The bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What are the four bases of spiritual power?"
The Buddha said:

"What is called the power of the basis of psychic potency consisting of concentration of desire and the exercise of volition: through it, one personally attains the basis of reflection, the basis of detachment from desire, and the basis of cessation, thereby embracing and subduing contentious debate;

the power of the basis of psychic potency consisting of concentration of exertion and the exercise of volition: through it, one personally attains the basis of reflection, the basis of detachment from desire, and the basis of cessation, thereby embracing and subduing contentious debate."

Possessing the power of the bases of psychic potency (ṛddhipāda) through concentration of mind and the application of effort, one attains for oneself a basis for reflection, a basis for detachment from desire, and a basis for cessation; therein one embraces and subdues contentious debate.

Possessing the power of the bases of psychic potency through concentration of observation and the application of effort, one observes for oneself the attainment of a basis for reflection, a basis for detachment from desire, and a basis for cessation; therein one embraces and subdues contentious debate.
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus! These are called the four bases of spiritual power."
The bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What are the five faculties?"
The Buddha said:
"They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
What is the faculty of faith?"
This refers to the arising of faith and aspiration toward cause and effect; within the cycle of saṃsāra, one possesses the right view of the distinctions in karmic retribution.

Whatever actions one performs—whether wholesome or unwholesome—one understands with genuine clarity, through the faculty of self-confidence, how each respective karmic fruit will be experienced as its corresponding retribution.
This is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*). What is the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*)?
It refers to generating faith and delight in the sublime Dharma, applying oneself with diligent effort, and practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
This is called the faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*). What is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*)?
By the power of vigor, one accumulates wholesome conduct, practicing it in every thought-moment without ever regressing.
This is called the faculty of mindfulness.
What is the faculty of concentration?
It refers to focusing the mind one-pointedly upon the recollection of dharmas, without distraction or agitation.
This is called the faculty of concentration.
What is the faculty of wisdom?
It refers to the unimpeded penetration and clear observation of all things within the state of concentration.
"This is called the faculty of wisdom.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha again, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"What are the five powers? The Buddha said,
"They are the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom."
What is the power of faith?
It refers to sentient beings who, having received the Dharma of the Tathāgata, take faith as their foundation; they are well-established therein and do not wander.
Whether it be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, devas, Māras, or Brahmās, or any worldly dharmas, they are able to believe and understand them, following and embracing them accordingly.
This is called the power of faith.
What is the power of diligence?

It refers to being able to be courageous and fierce, possessing firm and steadfast diligence, abiding securely in wholesome dharmas without weariness or indolence; though beset by manifold sufferings, one is able to endure them, not abandoning the yoke of the wholesome, and practicing great diligence.
This is called the power of diligence (*vīryabala*). What is the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*)?
It refers to abiding in a state of mindfulness, maintaining it with firm recollection, remaining constantly without distraction, and never forgetting.
This is called the power of mindfulness.
What is the power of concentration?
It refers to the ability to subdue unwholesome states, including the defilements of desire, karma, and its results, and even to abide in the four dhyānas and samādhis.
This is called the power of concentration.
What is the power of wisdom?

It refers to abiding in the world while giving rise to right wisdom, practicing the path of the noble ones with full cultivation, discerning unwholesome dharmas, and transcending the limits of all suffering.
"This is called the power of wisdom.
The bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What are the seven factors of enlightenment?
The Buddha said:

"They are the factor of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, the factor of enlightenment of diligence, the factor of enlightenment of pliancy, the factor of enlightenment of equanimity, and the factor of enlightenment of joy."
What is the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena?
It refers to the ability to discern among all phenomena by relying on reflection, relying on detachment from desire, and relying on cessation, thereby subduing disputes.
What is the awakening factor of mindfulness?
It refers to the cultivation of right mindfulness regarding all phenomena, based upon reflection, based upon detachment, and based upon cessation, for the purpose of subduing disputes.
What is the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
It refers to the ability to give rise to pure and sublime wisdom by contemplating the basis of renunciation, the basis of detachment, and the basis of cessation, thereby subduing all disputes.
What is the awakening factor of diligence?
It refers to being untiring in diligence regarding wholesome conduct, based upon reflection, based upon detachment from desire, and based upon cessation, for the purpose of subduing disputes.
What is the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

It refers to the removal of heaviness (*dausthulya*) regarding all phenomena, bringing the body and mind into a state of harmony and flexibility; it is based upon reflection, based upon detachment from desire, and based upon cessation, because it subdues all contention.
What is the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

It refers to being free from negligence regarding all phenomena, causing the mind to become tranquil, and relying upon reflection, reliance on dispassion, and reliance on cessation, thereby subduing disputes.
What is the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
It refers to the arising of the sensation of joy regarding all phenomena, based upon reflection, based upon detachment from desire, and based upon cessation, because it subdues disputes.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This is called the seven factors of enlightenment.
The bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the Eightfold Noble Path?
The Buddha said:
"They are right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
What is right view?"
Regarding the objects perceived, there is taking and giving;
there are wholesome and unwholesome actions;
and there are the fruits summoned by those wholesome and unwholesome actions.
There are all the karmic actions performed by sentient beings, both mundane and supramundane, up to and including the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship;

as well as subtle and excellent conduct in this world and the next—all of which he understands with perfect clarity through right view, purifies his holy life (*brahmacarya*), forever severs the obstacles of delusion, accomplishes what was to be done, and reaches the further shore.
This is called right view.
What is right intention?
It refers to discerning and selecting with wisdom so that the three karmas of body, speech, and mind are free from error and devoid of all faults.
This is called right intention.
What is right speech?
It refers to being able to permanently sever false speech, frivolous talk, harsh words, and divisive speech.
This is called right speech.
What is right action?
It refers to all sentient beings being forever free from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
This is called right action.
What is right livelihood?
It refers to receiving clothing, bedding, food and drink, and medicine from the world for the purpose of sustenance, and not through wrong livelihood.
This is called right livelihood. What is right effort?
It refers to being able to courageously destroy the demon of afflictions, constantly cultivating wholesome conduct, and remaining free from indolence.
This is called right effort.
What is right mindfulness?
It refers to recollecting the wholesome dharmas practiced in the past, maintaining them in every moment of thought without error.
This is called right mindfulness.
What is right concentration?
It refers to the mind being able to abide peacefully in śamatha and vipaśyanā, tranquil and unmoving.
"This is called right concentration.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This is called the Noble Eightfold Path."
At that time, the bhikṣu Vīryagambhīra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the sixteen mental recollections?”
The Buddha said:
"Because the mind of mindfulness is in harmony, one knows as it truly is that harmony is equanimity;
because the mind of mindfulness is in correspondence, one knows as it truly is that correspondence is equanimity."
Because one contemplates the self-nature of phenomena as being in conjunction, one knows with reality that this conjunction is equal;
because one contemplates the self-nature of phenomena as being in association, one knows with reality that this association is equal;
because one contemplates the growth of phenomena as being in conjunction, one knows with reality that this conjunction is equal.
Because mindfulness of phenomena increases through association, one understands as it truly is that association is equal;
because mindfulness of the body is conjoined with clear comprehension, one understands as it truly is that conjunction is equal;
because mindfulness of the body is associated with clear comprehension, one understands as it truly is that association is equal.
Because mindfulness of bodily activities is conjoined with clear comprehension, one understands as it truly is that they are conjoined and equal;
because mindfulness of bodily activities is associated with clear comprehension, one understands as it truly is that they are associated and equal.
Because mindfulness of the entire body is conjoined with correct awareness, one understands as it truly is that this conjunction is equal;
because mindfulness of the entire body is associated with correct awareness, one understands as it truly is that this association is equal;
because mindfulness of the activities of the entire body is conjoined with correct awareness, one understands as it truly is that this conjunction is equal.
Because mindfulness of all bodily formations is associated with clear comprehension, one understands as it truly is their association and equanimity;
because mindfulness of the pliancy of bodily formations is conjoined [with them], one understands as it truly is their conjunction and equanimity;
because mindfulness of the pliancy of bodily formations is associated [with them], one understands as it truly is their association and equanimity.
Because mindfulness, joy, and clear comprehension are conjoined, one knows as it truly is their equality of conjunction;
because mindfulness, joy, and clear comprehension are associated, one knows as it truly is their equality of association.
Because mindfulness, joy, and clear comprehension are in union, one understands as it truly is their equality in union;
because mindfulness, joy, and clear comprehension are in association, one understands as it truly is their equality in association.
Because mindfulness and clear comprehension are conjoined, one understands as it truly is that their conjunction is equal;
because mindfulness and clear comprehension are associated, one understands as it truly is that their association is equal.
Because mindfulness, mental activity, and clear comprehension are conjoined, one understands as it truly is their equality of conjunction;
because mindfulness, mental activity, and clear comprehension are associated, one understands as it truly is their equality of association.
Because the mental application of mindfulness, lightness, tranquility, and activity are in harmony, one understands as it truly is their equality in harmony;
because the mental application of mindfulness, lightness, tranquility, and activity are in accord, one understands as it truly is their equality in accord.
Because the mind is unified with joy and bliss, he understands as it truly is that unification is equal;
because the mind is associated with joy and bliss, he understands as it truly is that association is equal.
Because mindfulness and resolute conviction are conjoined with the mind, one knows as it truly is their equality of conjunction;
because mindfulness and resolute conviction are associated with the mind, one knows as it truly is their equality of association.
Because mindfulness and concentrated mind are conjoined, one knows as it truly is their equality of conjunction;
because mindfulness and concentrated mind are associated, one knows as it truly is their equality of association.

In this way, up to the contemplation of impermanence, the contemplation of dispassion, the contemplation of cessation, and the contemplation of renunciation, he understands them as they truly are in their harmony and equality;
he understands them as they truly are in their correspondence and equality.
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! These are called the sixteen mental recollections."
The bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the four fruits of the śrāvaka?”
The Buddha said:
“These are the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, and the fruit of arhat.
Regarding these four fruits, the assembly of śrāvakas is all able to believe and understand them; as for the ten titles of the Tathāgata, their merits are perfectly complete.”
They thoroughly understand the True Dharma, which is pure, widely disseminated, and inexhaustible;
they thoroughly understand the Saṅgha, which is endowed with manifold virtues and perfected in merit;
and they have attained complete realization of the principle of non-self.

With such faith and understanding, they purely cultivate the holy life, becoming endowed with precepts, concentration, wisdom, the analytical knowledges, and the liberation and knowledge and vision of liberation. They possess the supramundane merit of turning the wheel of the true Dharma and realize the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna), fully perfected in merit;
they realize the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin), fully perfected in merit;
and they realize the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmin), fully perfected in merit.
Having realized the fruit of Arhatship, his merits were fully perfected.

His pure precepts were complete, noble wisdom was manifest before him, and he dwelt in sovereign peace and security, free from all feverish afflictions. Pure and untainted, he remained uninterrupted until the end of the future, never regressing. With the wisdom of skillful means, he observed all things, attaining unimpeded penetration.
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! These are called the four fruits of the śrāvaka."
The bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are the ten powers of the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said:

That which is called the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), because one knows with perfect accuracy the correspondence and non-correspondence of cause and effect;
the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma (*karmasvakatā-jñānabala*), because one knows with perfect accuracy the three types of action throughout the three periods of time;

and the power of knowledge regarding meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and attainments (*dhyānavimokṣasamādhisamāpatti-jñānabala*), because one is able to know them all with perfect accuracy.

The power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties (*indriya*) is so called because one can fully comprehend whether the five faculties, such as faith and the rest, are weak, middling, or superior;
the power of knowing various inclinations (*adhimukti*) is so called because one can clearly perceive and thoroughly penetrate the inclinations regarding all phenomena;
and the power of knowing various elements (*dhātu*) is so called because one can fully comprehend the diverse elemental natures of immeasurable worlds.

The power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*), because it is able to fully comprehend all the various distinctions of the paths leading to all realms of existence;

the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-bala*), because it is able to fully comprehend the recollection of past lives and their objects throughout the past;

and the power of knowledge regarding birth and death (*cyutyupapāda-jñāna-bala*), because it is able to fully comprehend the causes and conditions for the birth and death of all classes of sentient beings.

"The power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*) is so called because the various afflictions, along with their underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), have been purified and exhausted without remainder.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"These are what are called the ten powers of the Tathāgata."
The bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are the four fearlessnesses?
The Buddha said:

Regarding the fearlessness of perfect enlightenment: because the Buddha has awakened to all phenomena as they truly are, having fully realized all dharmas with a mind free from fear, he is revered by gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, humans, and asuras alike.

Regarding the fearlessness of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows: because the Tathāgata’s outflows, sensual taints, and afflictions have all been exhausted, he dwells in a state of peace and security, free from alarm or dread; amidst the great assembly, he utters the lion’s roar, and is honored and praised by Brahmā, Śakra, the various devas, and the Cakravartin kings.

He possesses the fearlessness of having emerged from the obstacles to the path; for the Tathāgata has realized the noble paths of the three vehicles and is without obstruction regarding all phenomena, his mind is free from fear, and he is revered by all devas, māras, brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas.

He possesses the fearlessness of having emerged from the path to suffering; for the Tathāgata, having cultivated wholesome dharmas over incalculable eons, is able to definitively transcend the path of suffering, and he is revered by all devas, māras, brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“These are called the four fearlessnesses.
The bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What are the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence?
The Buddha said:

“They are the unimpeded eloquence regarding phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), the unimpeded eloquence regarding meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), the unimpeded eloquence regarding expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and the unimpeded eloquence regarding inspired speech (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).”
The unimpeded eloquence of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), because wisdom does not regress regarding untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*);
the unimpeded eloquence of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), because wisdom does not regress regarding the principles that are elucidated;
the unimpeded eloquence of language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), because one explains all the questions and difficulties of sentient beings with a single voice, causing them all to rejoice.
"Unimpeded eloquence means that one thoroughly penetrates all phenomena, both mundane and supramundane, because one's wisdom never regresses.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"These are called the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence."
The bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying,
“What are the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) of the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said:
"What is meant by this? It is that the Tathāgata has no errors, no harsh speech, and no diverse perceptions;
he has no unconcentrated mind, no loss of mindfulness, and no equanimity lacking discernment;
his desire does not diminish, his mindfulness does not diminish, his vigor does not diminish, his concentration does not diminish, his wisdom does not diminish, and his liberation does not diminish."
His bodily actions follow wisdom; his verbal actions follow wisdom; his mental actions follow wisdom.
He knows the past without attachment or obstruction; he knows the future without attachment or obstruction; he knows the present without attachment or obstruction.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"These are called the eighteen unique qualities.
The bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks? The Buddha said: "They are as follows:
the soles of the feet are level and full, with the high and low parts touching the ground equally."
The soles of his feet bear the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel with its hub and rim perfectly complete;
his hands and feet are soft and supple like *tūla* cotton;
and between the fingers and toes of his hands and feet there are webbed membranes, interlaced like gold.
The fingers and toes of his hands and feet are slender, long, and perfectly rounded;
his heels are broad and long, in proportion to his insteps;
and his insteps are high, full, and soft, in proportion to his heels.
His calves are slender and rounded, like those of the king of the eneya deer;
his arms are long and well-rounded, like the trunk of an elephant king, reaching below his knees when standing upright;
and his private parts are deeply concealed, like those of a dragon-elephant king.
From each and every pore of his body, a single hair grows; these hairs are soft, deep blue-black, and curl gracefully to the right.
His body hair points upward, is soft, deep blue-black, and curls to the right like a spiral.
His body is the color of pure gold, radiant and brilliant, adorned with all manner of jewels.
The skin is thin and lustrous, such that dust and grime do not adhere to it;
the palms of the hands, the soles of the feet, the nape of the neck, and both shoulders are characterized by the mark of the seven places being level and full;
and the area between the shoulders and the nape of the neck is characterized by being exquisitely well-filled.
The armpits are pure and completely full;
the countenance and deportment are perfect, upright, and exquisitely sublime;
the physical form is well-proportioned, broad, and straight, with all features in harmonious symmetry.
The proportions of his body’s height and breadth are equal in circumference, possessing the mark of being perfectly symmetrical like a nyagrodha tree;
the upper half of his body is like that of a lion king, possessing the mark of majestic and expansive presence;
and his body constantly emits light, with each side of his face extending one fathom, possessing the mark of the *vyāma-prabhā*.
He possesses forty teeth, which are even, level, clean, and closely set;
his four canine teeth are sharp and white, surpassing jade and snow;
and he possesses the mark of obtaining the supreme flavor among all tastes.
The mark of his tongue being broad and thin, which can completely cover his face;
the mark of his Brahma-voice being majestic and resonant, heard equally by all according to their capacity;
and the mark of his eyelashes being even and neat, like those of a bull king.
His eyes are deep azure, adorned with a bright white sclera and a crimson ring, possessing the mark of radiant purity;
his face is like the full moon, and his two eyebrows are bright and clean like the bow of Śakra, possessing the mark [of brows] like the bow of the Lord of Devas;
between his eyebrows is a white tuft of hair, curling to the right and spiraling gracefully like tūla-cotton, possessing the mark of brilliant, pure whiteness.
Upon his crown appears the *uṣṇīṣa*, lofty, prominent, and perfectly circular like the form of a celestial canopy.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Such are called the thirty-two marks.”
The Sūtra on the Definitive Meaning of the Dharma-Vehicle, Volume Middle;
The Sūtra on the Definitive Meaning of the Dharma-Vehicle, Volume Lower.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Mingyin Miaoshan Pujie.
Translated by Kumārajīva and others by imperial decree:
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣu Vīrasamudgata, saying:

"The thirty-two marks and the golden body manifested by the Tathāgata were all attained through the influence of various practices cultivated in the past; I shall now analyze and explain them for you as well."
Then the assembly of bhikṣus said:
"Indeed, listen attentively!
The Buddha spoke:

"It is because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, having practiced the bodhisattva path for immeasurable eons, were well-established and firm in their equanimity regarding the precepts, prohibitions, patience, and generosity, that they attained the mark of level and full soles."

Because he protected sentient beings from suffering through skillful means, was filial toward his parents, and adorned himself with generosity without ever regressing, he attained the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of his feet.

Because he served his elders and superiors by anointing their bodies, massaging them, providing baths and clothing, and supplying articles of adornment without ever turning back from these duties, he thereby attained the mark of soft and supple hands and feet.

By benefiting sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), protecting and mindful of them with impartiality and without distinction, he thereby attained the mark of golden webbing between the fingers and toes.

By being respectful and harmonious toward elders and superiors, by refraining from harming other sentient beings and from taking what is not given, and by being able to secretly protect living beings through the sublime Dharma, one thereby attains the mark of long, slender, and perfectly rounded fingers on the hands and feet.

By means of the wisdom of skillful means, he exhorts, guides, and protects all sentient beings, causing them to cultivate virtuous conduct without ever regressing; consequently, he attains the mark of broad heels that are proportionate to the insteps, and the mark of high, full, and soft insteps that are proportionate to the heels.

Because he has personally and correctly embraced the True Dharma, understood it as it truly is, extensively expounded it for others, and properly served as a benefactor to others, he has attained the mark of calves that are slender, rounded, and like those of the eneya deer king.

By practicing virtuous deeds without weariness or indolence, causing all wholesome dharmas to increase progressively, one thereby attains the mark of having arms that are well-developed, rounded, straight, and reaching below the knees.

Because he was able to compassionately embrace with the True Dharma those sentient beings who had been expelled by others and were without refuge, causing them to know shame and remorse, he has attained the mark of having private parts deep and concealed like those of a dragon-elephant king.

Because he has personally observed with wisdom and is virtuous and excellent, because he delights in desiring to associate with those who dwell in solitude, because he relies upon a single factor, because he has entered into the profound meaning, and because he is able to eliminate adventitious defilements, he attains the mark of having a single hair growing from each pore—soft, deep blue-black, and curling to the right—and the mark of his hair and body-hair being directed upward, soft, deep blue-black, and spiraling to the right like a conch shell.

Being able to bestow the food and drink of the joy of the Dharma that delights the mind, as well as vehicles, clothing, ornaments, and various articles for sustaining the body, and being forever free from ill will, one thereby attains a body of true golden color, with skin so thin and supple that dust and grime do not adhere to it.

By extensively bestowing exquisite delicacies, food, and drink upon all sentient beings so that they were all fully satisfied, he thereby brought about the mark of his body having seven parts that are all perfectly full and level.

In accordance with the needs of sentient beings, he acts as they arise in a manner consistent with the Dharma; he serves as their leader and companion, free from the conceit of "I" and without a harsh or unruly mind. He is able to bring about beneficial matters for sentient beings, and by virtue of this, he attains the mark of having the upper half of his body like that of a lion king.

He is by nature courageous and resolute in all matters; furthermore, he has attained the perfection of his shoulders and neck, his upper arms and armpits are full, his deportment is dignified and majestic, and his physical form is well-proportioned and expansive.

One is able to guard one's own actions of body, speech, and mind; provides excellent medicine to those afflicted by illness; does not engage in any form of unequal or improper activity; and brings about harmony among the elements that are in mutual conflict. By these means, one attains a physical form as perfectly proportioned as a nyagrodha tree and a constant radiance extending one fathom.

By staying far away from all speech that destroys friendships or causes estrangement, and by skillfully reconciling those who have already become alienated through wholesome words, one thereby attains the mark of having forty teeth that are even, level, clean, and closely set.
By cultivating vast loving-kindness and contemplating the meaning of the Dharma, he obtained four fangs that were sharp and white, surpassing snow or jade.

Out of compassion for sentient beings as if they were his only child, he protected them through skillful means and provided them with medicine; by this, he obtained the supreme sense of taste among all flavors.

Because he remained far removed from killing and cultivated a mind of loving-kindness, and because he was able to practice correctly within the vast Dharma, he attained as his karmic fruit the appearance of an *uṣṇīṣa* upon his crown and a tongue that is broad and thin, extending so as to cover the entire circumference of his face.

By constantly practicing truthful speech, affectionate speech, speech in accordance with the Dharma, and pleasing speech, one attains the great Brahma-voice through these causes and conditions; one's words are refined and elegant, capable of delighting the minds of all.
In all worlds, he practiced great compassion, showing pity for and benefiting all sentient beings; by virtue of this, he obtained eyes of deep blue color and eyelashes like those of a bull king.

Seeing those with virtue, one praises them according to reality and extols their excellence; by this, one obtains a face like the full moon, eyebrows like the bow of Indra, and a white tuft of hair between the brows that curls gracefully, pure and brilliant white like *tūla* cotton.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In this way, you should understand the past causes and conditions for the thirty-two marks of the Buddhas.
The bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are the eighty secondary marks of the World-Honored One?
The Buddha said: "They are as follows:
the World-Honored One’s fingernails are narrow and long, thin, moist, lustrous, and pure."
The World-Honored One’s fingers are slender, rounded, and straight;
the World-Honored One’s hands and feet have fingers that are equal in length with well-filled and closely set interstices;
the World-Honored One’s bone joints are deeply recessed and not visible.
The World-Honored One’s hands and feet are supple and soft;
the World-Honored One’s sinews and veins are coiled and deeply hidden;
the World-Honored One’s two ankles are both concealed and not visible.
The World-Honored One’s gait is measured and dignified, like that of a dragon-elephant king;
the World-Honored One’s movements are elegant and refined, like those of a royal swan;
when the World-Honored One turns his head to look back, his entire body rotates along with him, just like a dragon-elephant king.
The limbs and joints of the World-Honored One are plump and rounded, perfectly and beautifully arranged;
the World-Honored One’s countenance is dignified and serene, free from any fear;
the World-Honored One’s body and members are stable and composed, without any agitation or restlessness.
The joints of the World-Honored One’s limbs are interlocked without gaps, like a coiled dragon;
the World-Honored One’s kneecaps are perfectly round and exquisite;
the World-Honored One’s private parts are pure and free from defilement.
The limbs and joints of the World-Honored One are dense and firm;
the physical form of the World-Honored One is majestic and dignified on all sides;
the radiance of the World-Honored One’s body constantly illuminates itself.
The World-Honored One’s navel is deep, perfectly round, and exceptionally marvelous;
the World-Honored One’s navel is thick, neither sunken nor protruding;
the World-Honored One’s body is radiant, pure, and free from defilement.
The Blessed One’s skin is free from warts and growths;
the Blessed One’s palms are flat, full, and lustrous;
the Blessed One’s abdomen is square, soft, and supple.
The lines on the World-Honored One’s palms are deep, long, clear, straight, and unbroken;
the color of the World-Honored One’s lips is a radiant crimson, like the *bimba* fruit;
the World-Honored One’s face is like the full moon, dignified and perfectly proportioned.
The Blessed One’s tongue is broad and long, completely covering his face;
the Blessed One’s Brahma-voice is perfect and full, like a celestial drum;
the Blessed One’s nose is high and straight, its nostrils not visible.
The Blessed One’s teeth are square, even, and closely set;
the Blessed One’s four canine teeth are sharp, brilliant, and white;
the Blessed One’s eyes are pure, deep blue, with the blue and white clearly distinguished.
The World-Honored One’s eyes are long and wide, like the petals of a blue lotus;
the World-Honored One’s upper and lower eyelashes are even, dense, and thick;
the World-Honored One’s eyebrows are not white, but are long, fine, smooth, and soft.
The upper half of the World-Honored One’s body is majestic and most excellent, like that of a lion king;
the World-Honored One’s forehead is broad and full, level, even, and sublime;
the World-Honored One’s ears are thick and long, with well-rounded lobes.
The World-Honored One’s two ears are exquisite and symmetrical, free from all defects;
the World-Honored One’s countenance causes those who behold it to feel neither aversion nor defilement, but to give rise to reverence in all;
the World-Honored One’s eyebrows are elegantly arched and well-ordered, their color a deep azure-blue.
The World-Honored One’s eyebrows are high-arched, radiant, and lustrous, like the crescent moon;
the World-Honored One’s hair is deep blue-black and long, dense and free from gray;
the World-Honored One’s hair is fragrant, pure, fine and soft, glossy, and curls to the right.
The World-Honored One’s hair on his head is even and well-arranged, radiant and pure;
the World-Honored One’s hair on his head is firm and does not fall out;
the World-Honored One’s hair on his head is free from dust and grime.
The body of the World-Honored One is full and firm;
the physical proportions of the World-Honored One are well-developed, long, and straight;
all the orifices of the World-Honored One are pure and exquisite.
The physical marks and majestic power of the World-Honored One are preeminent, with none equal to him;
the physical marks of the World-Honored One are such that all delight in gazing upon them, never tiring of doing so;
the World-Honored One’s countenance is well-proportioned in its length and breadth, pure and radiant like the full moon in autumn.
The World-Honored One’s countenance is serene and radiant; he smiles and speaks first, facing others rather than turning his back.
The World-Honored One’s face is lustrous and joyful, free from frowns, and devoid of any bluish or reddish hue.
The World-Honored One’s limbs are pure and stainless, and likewise free from any foul odor.
From every pore of the World-Honored One’s body, there constantly issues forth subtle and wondrous fragrances that fulfill all wishes;
from the World-Honored One’s mouth, there constantly issues forth the most supreme and excellent fragrance;
and the World-Honored One’s crown is perfectly round and exquisite, like a celestial canopy.
The Blessed One’s body hairs are radiant, pure, and deep blue, like the neck of a peacock, with crimson luster intermingled in exquisite patterns;
the Blessed One’s Dharma voice is heard equally by all according to their capacity, responding to principle without error;
and the Blessed One’s cranial protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) is such that no one can see its top.
The joints of the fingers and toes of the World-Honored One’s hands and feet are distinct, adorned, and exquisite;
when the World-Honored One walks, his feet remain four finger-widths above the ground, yet the marks of the wheels appear;
the World-Honored One maintains himself without requiring the protection of others, his body neither swaying nor staggering.
The World-Honored One’s majestic virtue resounds afar, such that those with minds of anger see joy and those who are terrified find peace;
the World-Honored One’s voice is neither too high nor too low, speaking with harmony and delight in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings;
the World-Honored One is able to observe the various classes of sentient beings and preach the Dharma according to their speech, sounds, and mental dispositions.
The World-Honored One expounds all dharmas with a single voice, yet each sentient being attains understanding according to their own kind;
the World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma always follows a sequential order, for there must be causes and conditions, and his words are never unwholesome;
the World-Honored One regards all classes of sentient beings with equanimity, praising the good and censuring the evil without partiality or hatred.
The Blessed One acts only after first observing, being fully endowed with exemplary conduct so as to bring about clear understanding and purity;
the Blessed One’s marks and signs cannot be fully perceived by any sentient beings;
the Blessed One’s skull bone is firm, solid, and perfectly rounded.
“The Blessed One’s countenance shows no signs of aging;
the palms of his hands, the soles of his feet, and the area between his shoulders all bear the auspicious mark of the *śrīvatsa*.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“Such are what are called the eighty minor marks.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken this sutra, he further addressed the bhikṣu Vīrasāgara, saying:

“The wondrous principles and definitive meanings of the Dharma-vehicle that I have now taught—the essential teachings they expound—are good in the beginning, middle, and end, providing benefit and peace.”

You have skillfully recited, upheld, expounded, analyzed, and explained [the Dharma], guiding sentient beings to cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*). You eat but one meal a day in accordance with the Dharma, possess the three robes in full, and dwell in open spaces, or among burial mounds, or beneath forest trees, or in secluded places. You practice the dhūta austerities, remaining constantly diligent and energetic without indolence, forever free from the defilement of delusions, and attaining ultimate liberation.

At that time, the bhikṣu Vīryagambhīra, together with the great bhikṣus who had assembled there, as well as the entire multitude of devas, humans, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced, paid homage, and faithfully accepted and practiced it.
